content:
Moving keyboard shortcuts onto a programmable macro keyboard has been the most effective productivity boost I've ever done.

Keyboard shortcuts exploration journey

My initial foray into keyboard shortcuts began with the simple text replacement feature in macOS — using @@ for my primary email address, and similar shortcuts for entering my full name, address, phone number, zip code, and more.

I then decided to upgrade, setting up shortcuts through Keyboard Maestro to directly open my most frequently used folders and applications.

From Desktop to Downloads, and work-related folders, hitting Fn+F1 through Fn+F6 has become pure muscle memory, taking me to places that used to require several mouse clicks. The other function keys open my favourite applications and websites, as well as Keyboard Maestro's clipboard history switcher.

I then began further automating my workflow, including opening QuickTime and starting a new recording, as well as automatically launching Shure PlusMOTI when plugging in a specific USB-C microphone.

Before long, I also customised shortcuts for Adobe Audition's tools, settings, and panel configurations — some of which I quickly moved to the Logitech MX Master mouse for even faster editing.

Taking it further

This setup worked well for a long time, until one day my 9to5Mac colleague Gui Rambo introduced me to a small macro keyboard he had purchased, featuring 12 buttons and 3 knobs. I was immediately intrigued and bought the same one.

Right out of the box, I discovered it required additional configuration to work properly on macOS. Fortunately, a GitHub project handled all the complicated parts for me, while ChatGPT took care of the rest.

One advantage of this setup is having a dedicated keyboard for triggering Keyboard Maestro shortcuts, which means I don't have to memorise them, nor worry about ergonomic issues.

Furthermore, because this keyboard can provide up to 3 layers of 12 buttons each, and the knobs can also be pressed as buttons, I can use one mode of operation when working in Adobe Audition, and an entirely different mode when working at the operating system level.

When working in Adobe Audition, this macro keyboard paired with the MX Master mouse allows me to quickly switch tools, export files (or export just the selection), apply various effects such as normalisation, compression, de-reverb, de-essing, ripple delete, and more — orders of magnitude faster than using regular keyboard shortcuts, let alone no shortcuts at all, and the workflow is much smoother.

At the operating system level, I can switch the same keyboard to another layer and just as easily switch audio inputs, adjust volume, tweak screen brightness, mute and unmute the microphone, and open frequently used folders.

Honestly, it took me a while to remember all these commands, but they became habits faster than I expected. More importantly, when I have to work in an environment without this setup, frankly, my Mac feels broken to me.

What's more, macro keyboards come in all sorts of configurations and choices — shapes, sizes, buttons, knobs, light colours — you name it. This field really feels like endless exploration. If your work involves any repetitive actions (and whose doesn't?), I wholeheartedly recommend giving it a try yourself.
